origin_region: Sri Lanka · a few factories in several districts
cultivar: Assam-type seedling bushes and TRI clones
processing: Steamed or pan-fired to prevent oxidation, rolled (often tightly into gunpowder-style pellets or twisted into 'Young Hyson' leaf) and dried; made mostly for export, much of it to Middle Eastern and North African markets.
appearance_dry: Tight dark-green pellets (gunpowder) or twisted greyish-green leaf.
appearance_wet: Olive to khaki leaf, somewhat coarse.
taste_profile: Bold and brisk for a green: toasty, lightly nutty and vegetal with a pronounced drying finish; made for sweet mint tea rather than solo sipping.

brewing.notes: Alone, keep it cool and short; or brew it strong with fresh mint and sugar, Moroccan style.

vintage_note: Sold through the Colombo auction by grade (Gunpowder, Young Hyson, Chun Mee, Sowmee, GP Special) with no vintage marketing, plus a few estate lots under their own name; buy the current year's lot and use it within the year, as the greens stale faster than the island's black teas.
description:
Ceylon green tea is Sri Lanka's smaller, less famous green line, made by a small number of factories mostly for export, much of it to Middle Eastern and North African markets where it goes into sweet mint tea. It is a bold, toasty green rather than a delicate one, and that is by design: it has to stand up to sugar and mint in a Moroccan glass.

The leaf is steamed or pan-fired to stop oxidation, then rolled, often tightly into gunpowder-style pellets, or twisted into 'Young Hyson' leaf, and dried. Assam-type leaf makes a stronger, more astringent green than Chinese bushes, and Sri Lankan factories lean into that.

Brewed on its own the cup is yellow to pale amber-green, toasty, nutty and vegetal with a pronounced drying finish. Keep the water around 80 °C and the steeps short, or do what most of its buyers do: brew it strong, add fresh mint and sugar, and pour it from a height.

It is sold through the Colombo auction by grade (Gunpowder, Young Hyson, Chun Mee, Sowmee, GP Special) with no vintage marketing, and a few estates sell small lots under their own name. Buy the current year's lot and use it within the year; greens stale faster than the island's black teas.

Not the green tea to start with if you are new to green tea, but a very good one for Moroccan-style mint tea.
